name: localtunnel (localtunnel/localtunnel)
last_commit_or_release_date: Last commit Aug 29, 2025 (README-only doc fix); last real functional commit/release Aug 2022 (v2.0.2 published to npm ~5 years ago, per npm page); most of the meaningful commit history stops around 2021-2022.
maturity_notes: Very popular historically but effectively in maintenance-only mode: recent commits are trivial README/link fixes, not feature or security work. npm package hasn't shipped a new version in ~5 years. The public hosted server (localtunnel.me) is known to be unreliable/overloaded (frequent community reports of downtime), and the project explicitly documents that a *separate* localtunnel/server repo powers the tunnel server, which is not actively developed either. Red flag: relying on the free public localtunnel.me service is not viable for a production feature; self-hosting the aging server code is possible but you inherit unmaintained infra code.
popularity_signal: 22.5k GitHub stars, 1.6k forks, 408 npm dependents, decades-long name recognition as the original Node localtunnel port; still widely referenced in tutorials/StackOverflow.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: The npm 'localtunnel' package is CLIENT-only (a library you import to dial OUT to a tunnel server) - it does not export a server module. To use it for OUR use case (llama-server on user machine calling out, cloud SvelteKit backend receiving), the CLIENT side would run on the user's machine, but the SERVER side requires deploying and running the separate 'localtunnel/server' Node project as its own process/binary (its own HTTP+TCP listener, subdomain routing, port pool) - it cannot be mounted as a middleware inside an existing Express/SvelteKit adapter-node HTTP server. This means significant infra lift: a dedicated always-on server process, subdomain/DNS management, and monitoring, in addition to our own SvelteKit backend.
client_side_simplicity: Client is simple and unprivileged: `npm install -g localtunnel` or `npx localtunnel --port N`, or `require('localtunnel')` programmatically. No admin/root or network interface changes needed; runs as an ordinary user-space Node process.
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Rough integration LOC: ~50-150 lines to wire the client into our Python-wrapping Node bridge or a small Node sidecar, PLUS 300-500+ lines/hours of ops work to deploy, harden, and monitor the separate localtunnel server (subdomain routing, TLS termination, port allocation, uptime monitoring) since it cannot live inside our existing SvelteKit process. Ongoing burden: we would own and operate a second stateful service instead of one, largely defeating the 'minimize infra' goal.
viability_notes: The client library is easy and requires no admin rights, but the server-side is a separate unmaintained process we'd have to self-host and operate ourselves - it cannot be embedded in our existing SvelteKit/Node backend. Given our priority of minimal infra and no separate relay server, this adds real operational burden for a codebase that isn't being actively developed anymore.

name: Tunnelmole (robbie-cahill/tunnelmole-client)
license: Client: MIT. Hosted service/server: AGPLv3 (per README FAQ).
last_commit_or_release_date: npm package 'tunnelmole' v2.4.0 published ~1 year ago; repo has 353 commits total, active-looking commit cadence historically (exact latest commit date not directly confirmed beyond npm's 'a year ago' publish marker).
maturity_notes: Actively maintained relative to the older localtunnel forks - has CI, tests, telemetry/crash-reporting infra, a dashboard, and a companion self-hostable service repo (tunnelmole-service). Single-maintainer (Robbie Cahill) project, so bus-factor risk exists. Ships default telemetry (opt-out via env var) which is a minor privacy/ops consideration to disclose to end users.
popularity_signal: 1.9k GitHub stars, 124 forks, 17 npm dependents, actively promoted as an 'open source ngrok alternative'; has a marketing site (tunnelmole.com) and paid subscription tier for custom subdomains, suggesting a sustainable maintenance incentive.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: Same architectural pattern as localtunnel: the 'tunnelmole' npm package installed via `npm install tunnelmole` exposes a CLIENT API (`import { tunnelmole } from 'tunnelmole'`) that runs on the machine being exposed (would run alongside llama-server locally) - it dials out to a hosted or self-hosted tunnel SERVER. The server component lives in a separate repo, 'tunnelmole-service', which must be run as its own process (their own hosted multi-tenant service, or self-hosted equivalent) - again NOT embeddable as a library inside our existing SvelteKit/Express HTTP server. Same infra burden pattern as localtunnel.
client_side_simplicity: Client install is simple and unprivileged for the JS path: `npm install --save tunnelmole` then `import { tunnelmole } from 'tunnelmole'; const url = await tunnelmole({port: N})`. Note the docs show `sudo npm install -g tunnelmole` for the CLI, but that's only needed for GLOBAL install convention (writing to system npm dir) - a local/project-scoped install or the precompiled binaries avoids sudo entirely. No network interface/root access required for tunnel operation itself.
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Similar to localtunnel: ~50-150 LOC of glue to invoke the client API programmatically from our Python-wrapping process (would need an embedded Node runtime or a small sidecar since tunnelmole is Node-only), plus running/monitoring the separate tunnelmole-service (or paying for the hosted one, at which point we're dependent on a single-maintainer commercial-ish service with usage limits). If we rely on the free hosted tunnelmole.net service, we avoid running our own server but introduce a hard external dependency and no SLA.
viability_notes: More actively maintained than plain localtunnel, but architecturally identical: still a Node-only client + separately-run server, not embeddable in our SvelteKit backend process. Reliance on either a single-maintainer hosted service or self-hosting yet another relay server conflicts with our 'minimal infra, no separate binary' priority.

name: pipenet (punkpeye/pipenet)
license: See repo LICENSE file (README does not explicitly restate it in extracted text; repo shows a generic 'License' link, not confirmed MIT/other - flag as unverified pending direct file check).
last_commit_or_release_date: 44 commits total on main branch; younger, smaller project (exact last-commit date not directly extracted, but repo is recent/modern per its ESM+TS tooling and its stated purpose of supporting current MCP tooling).
maturity_notes: Newer and smaller community than localtunnel/tunnelmole (527 stars, single primary author 'punkpeye'/Frank Fiegel, sponsored by glama.ai), but explicitly positioned and marketed as an actively-maintained, modernized fork of localtunnel with TypeScript, ESM, and - critically - cloud-deployment-friendly single-port mode designed for exactly our scenario (running the tunnel server inside a container/PaaS with limited exposed ports). No long track record yet, so lower confidence in long-term maintenance, but design intent aligns very closely with our needs.
popularity_signal: 527 GitHub stars, 24 forks; used internally to power punkpeye's own 'mcp-proxy' project (a well-known MCP tool), lending some credibility; not yet as widely known as localtunnel/tunnelmole outside the MCP/AI tooling niche.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: This is the key differentiator: pipenet ships BOTH client and server as importable JS/TS APIs in one npm package. Server side: `import { createServer } from 'pipenet/server'; const server = createServer({...}); server.listen(3000)` - this returns a Node http.Server-like object that can be embedded directly alongside (or wrapped by) our existing SvelteKit adapter-node server, or run as an internal service within our Node/Express backend, with lifecycle hooks (onTunnelCreated, onTunnelClosed, onRequest) that let us integrate auth/logging into our own request pipeline. It also explicitly supports 'single shared tunnel port' mode for containerized/cloud deployments (fly.io/Docker/K8s) which matches how our SvelteKit backend is likely deployed. Client side: `import { pipenet } from 'pipenet'; const tunnel = await pipenet({port: 3000, host: 'https://our-server.com'})` runs on the user's local machine to dial into our own server - no third-party hosted dependency needed at all since we run the server ourselves as part of our own infra.
client_side_simplicity: Fully unprivileged: `npm install pipenet` then `npx pipenet client --port 3000` or the programmatic client API. No admin/root, no network interface configuration, no daemon installation - pure JS library that 'just works' per the README's explicit zero-setup design goal (contrasted against zrok, which needs CLI-based environment init).
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Because the server is a library, not a separate binary, integration is much lighter: rough estimate ~150-300 LOC to mount pipenet's createServer alongside/within our existing Node HTTP server, wire the lifecycle hooks into our auth/session/routing layer, and adapt single-port tunnel mode to our deployment target. Client-side glue for the local llama-server wrapper: ~50-100 LOC. Ongoing admin burden is much lower than the previous two options: no separate always-on relay service to operate, since the tunnel server logic runs inside our own already-running Node/SvelteKit process; only need to manage our own domain(s) and monitor the process we already monitor.
viability_notes: Best architectural fit for our stated priorities: server is an embeddable library (not a separate binary) that can live inside our existing SvelteKit/Node backend, was purpose-built for cloud/single-port deployments, and the client requires zero admin/root on the user's machine. Since the local wrapper is not constrained to Python, client and server can share the same npm package and runtime with no cross-language reimplementation. Main caveats are its youth (527 stars, small single-maintainer-ish project, only 44 commits) and unconfirmed long-term maintenance, plus needing to double check its exact license terms before adopting.

name: progrium/localtunnel (original, unmaintained)
language: Go (current v3 rewrite); earlier historical versions in Ruby+Python Twisted (v1) and Python gevent (v2)
last_commit_or_release_date: Repo is explicitly archived-in-spirit: README states the project 'fell into obscurity' after being copied by commercial successors (notably ngrok). Current master is a minimal (<200 line) Go v3 rewrite built on the author's 'Duplex' library; no public server exists for it; 185 total commits across the repo's whole multi-decade history (prototype 2010, v1 2010, v2 2011-2013, v3 unspecified/dormant).
maturity_notes: Explicitly and openly declared unmaintained/legacy by its own author (progrium/Jeff Lindsay) in the README itself - the repo is kept mainly to archive project history, not for active use. v3 has 'no public server' set up and 'the scope of the project is pretty fixed where it is,' i.e., the author does not intend further development. This is the clearest maintenance red flag of all four options.
popularity_signal: 3.2k stars, 243 forks - notable mainly for historical/pioneering significance (it inspired ngrok and the entire localtunnel.me lineage), not for current active usage. Little to no real popularity signal as a currently-adopted tool.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: Not applicable to a Node.js/SvelteKit integration at all in its current form: it is a Go program/library (via the author's Duplex framework), requires `go install` to build, and has no npm package, no JS bindings, and 'no public server' set up. Embedding it in our Node/SvelteKit backend would require either shelling out to a compiled Go binary as a separate process, or a full reimplementation in Node using the underlying protocol/design ideas - there is no library import path applicable to a JS project.
client_side_simplicity: Would require installing/building a Go binary (`go install github.com/progrium/localtunnel`) on the end-user's machine - the client isn't distributed as prebuilt cross-platform binaries yet per the README ('Binary releases have not been set up yet'), so a typical non-technical end user would need Go tooling installed, which is a meaningfully higher and impractical bar than an npm-installable JS tool. Does not require admin/root or network interface changes, but the installation friction itself is a real usability problem for our target users.
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Effectively not integratable as-is for a Node/SvelteKit stack without either (a) building/shipping a separate Go binary per platform (packaging + distribution burden, comparable to or worse than a custom protocol), or (b) treating this only as a design reference and reimplementing similar ideas ourselves in Node - which is essentially what our own APLC-1 protocol already plans to do. No 'server as embeddable library' option exists since no server implementation is currently published/maintained for v3 at all.
viability_notes: Explicitly unmaintained by its own author, written in Go with no npm/JS bindings, no distributed public server, and no prebuilt cross-platform client binaries - it offers essentially zero direct integration value for a Node/SvelteKit stack beyond historical/architectural inspiration. Not viable as an off-the-shelf dependency; at best it's a design reference for our custom APLC-1 protocol.
